<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   • NocoBase is a full‐stack, extensibility‐first no‐code development platform implemented as a single monorepo.  
   • It consists of a Node.js/TypeScript backend (server and CLI), a React/TypeScript frontend (client), and a set of first‐class plugins.  
   • Purpose: let users define data models, UI blocks, and workflows without code, but support deep extensibility via plugins.  

2. Analyze the file structure  
   • Top-level directories:  
     - packages/core – core libraries segmented by function (app, auth, cli, client, server, database, cache, telemetry, etc.)  
     - packages/presets – opinionated presets for quick starts  
     - packages/plugins – first-party plugins (ACL, actions, charts, workflows, notification, etc.)  
     - examples – small demo apps  
     - docker, docker-compose.yml – Docker images for various databases and full stack  
     - .github/workflows – CI/CD pipelines for build, test, release  
   • Monorepo with Lerna & Yarn Workspaces: each package/plugins has its own package.json, source, tests.  
   • Key configuration: tsconfig.json, Dockerfiles, CI workflows, .env.example for env vars.  

3. Inspect the README for insights  
   • Architecture overview: “plugin architecture,” “data model‐driven,” “WYSIWYG UI configuration”  
   • Technologies: Koa/Express style server core, Sequelize or custom database layer, React + Ant Design frontend, Umi/Dumi for docs.  

4. System design diagram guidance  
   a. Main components (boxes):  
      • CLI (packages/core/cli & create-nocobase) – development & deployment commands  
      • Server core (packages/core/server) – HTTP API, plugin loader, lifecycle manager, gateway (IPC/WS)  
      • Plugin modules (packages/plugins/@nocobase/*) – server and client extensions loaded at runtime  
      • Client app (packages/core/app/client) – React SPA, dynamic schema rendering, plugin UIs, WebSocket client  
      • Database layer (packages/core/database & packages/core/data-source-manager) – ORM, multi-DB support  
      • Cache/Lock/Telemetry (packages/core/cache, lock-manager, telemetry)  
      • External services – SMTP (notification-email), SMS providers, AI providers, object storage (file-manager)  
   b. Relationships and interactions (arrows):  
      • CLI → Server (spawn subprocess, send commands, init DB, manage migrations)  
      • Server ←→ Database (ORM calls, migrations)  
      • Server ←→ Cache/Lock/Telemetry (cache reads/writes, metrics)  
      • Client ↔ Server API (REST/GraphQL over HTTP)  
      • Client ←→ Server via WebSocket (real-time UI updates, pub-sub)  
      • Plugin modules ↔ Server core (register routes, resource actions, middleware)  
      • Plugin modules ↔ Client (register UI schema initializers, settings panels)  
      • Server ↔ External services (SMTP, SMS, AI APIs, file storage backends)  
   c. Architectural patterns and principles:  
      • Plugin architecture – dynamic discovery/registration of modules on both client and server  
      • Monolith modularization – clear separation into core packages vs business plugins  
      • Data-driven UI – UI schema stored in DB and driven by server API, rendering components dynamically  
      • CQRS-style separation between resource actions (resourcer) and data layer (database, data-source manager)  
   d. Relevant technologies & frameworks:  
      • Backend: TypeScript, Koa-like plugin server, Sequelize-style ORM, Lerna, Docker  
      • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Ant Design, Umi/Dumi, dynamic schema components  
      • DevOps: GitHub Actions, Docker Compose, Gitpod integration  

5. Tailoring the diagram for this full-stack, plugin-driven architecture  
   • Emphasize the separation:  
     - Frontend SPA vs API server vs database  
     - Plugin manager layer between server core and plugins  
     - Independent plugin packages loaded into both client and server  
   • Show data flow:  
     - How UI schema changes in DB propagate to client via API  
     - How plugins extend server routes and client UI blocks  
   • Highlight extensibility:  
     - Plugins as first-class boxes hooking into core extension points  

6. Diagram elements and styling  
   • Boxes with clear labels: “CLI,” “Server Core,” “Plugin Manager,” “Plugin X,” “Client SPA,” “Database,” “Cache,” “External Services.”  
   • Arrows with direction:   
     - Solid line for request/response (Client→Server→DB→Server→Client)  
     - Dashed line for eventing/pub-sub (WebSocket, internal bus)  
     - Dotted line for asynchronous tasks (workflow engine, telemetry)  
   • Color coding/shapes:  
     - Core (blue rectangles), Plugins (green rectangles), Infrastructure (gray cylinders for DB/Cache), External (orange clouds).  
   • Annotations:  
     - Note technology stacks inside components (e.g., “Koa + TypeScript,” “React + AntD”).  
     - Mark dynamic plugin loading flow.  

7. Detail-level guidance  
   • Capture each essential sub-component without overcrowding: aggregate related packages under one box (e.g., “Database Layer: core/database + core/data-source-manager”).  
   • Show plugin lifecycle: discovery → registration → execution.  
   • Indicate CI/CD via GitHub Actions and Docker builds.  
   • If space permits, include a mini “build/deploy” pipeline to show how images are built, e2e tests run, and deployments triggered.  

Use these guidelines to create a detailed, accurate system design diagram that reflects NocoBase’s monorepo structure, plugin architecture, and full-stack interactions. Ensure labels, arrows, and colors make component boundaries and data flows crystal clear.  
</explanation>
